                 LIMITED REQUEST FOR REHEARING AND CLARIFICATION
                     OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

           Constellation submits this limited request for rehearing and clarification of the June 2026

Co-Location Order.1 We raise four discrete points on rehearing to reinforce the Commission’s

objective of establishing sufficiently clear tariff terms to allow the speedy connection and service

to Co-Located Loads in a way that “facilitate[s] more efficient use of the existing transmission

system” and “limit[s] unnecessary transmission system buildout” in PJM.2




1
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 (2026) (“June 2026 Co-Location Order”).
2
    Id. P 579; see also PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 160 (2025) (“December 2025 Co-Location
     Order”) (“These new transmission service options reflect a Co-Located Load’s ability to limit withdrawals from the
     transmission system and potentially avoid costly and inefficient transmission system buildout that may not be
     necessary.”).
            First, the Commission should modify the June 2026 Co-Location Order to require study

deadlines, which are the most critical path for the speedy interconnection of Co-Located Loads

and would be logically consistent with the ANOPR Show Cause Order.3

           Second, the Commission should require PJM to spell out in its Tariff the methodology and

process (including deadlines) for completing Necessary Studies. These terms belong in the Tariff,

and not the Manuals, because they “significantly affect rates, terms, and conditions” of service and

are “readily susceptible to specification.”4

           Third, the Commission should modify the operational penalty for the misoperation of

control technologies and/or protections to include only a two-strike disqualification as opposed to

a 120-day suspension on top of a two-strike disqualification. A 120-day suspension has no added

reliability benefit, is inconsistent with existing practice, and could have a chilling effect that could

result in costly and unnecessary Network Upgrades.

           Fourth, as Constellation recommended, the Commission should mitigate Transmission

Owners’ proposals that give them unfettered discretion over the timelines and technical

requirements for necessary control technologies and/or protection systems. The Commission

should also require all Transmission Owner standards, requirements, guidance, and practices

related to necessary control technologies and/or protection schemes for Co-Location

Arrangements to be on file with the Commission.5 The Commission failed to articulate its

reasoning for rejecting these recommendations, rendering its decision arbitrary and capricious.




3
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 (2026) (“ANOPR Show Cause Order”).
4
    Energy Storage Ass’n v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 162 FERC ¶ 61,296, at P 103 (2018) (citing Cal. Indep. Sys.
    Operator Corp., 122 FERC ¶ 61,271, at P 16 (2008)).
5
    Response Brief of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 et al., at 10-12 (Apr. 24, 2026)
    (“Constellation Apr. 24 Response Brief”).

                                                          2
            In addition, Constellation seeks clarification, or in the alternative, rehearing on the

Commission’s denial of Constellation’s request to modify the definition of Co-Located Load

Generating Facility so that only the portion of the Generating Facility serving the Co-Located Load

be considered the Co-Located Generating Facility. When only a portion of a Generating Facility’s

capacity is dedicated to serving co-located non-network load (say, a 100 MW non-network load is

co-located with a 500 MW generator), then only that portion should be considered a Co-Located

Generating Facility and required to delist. Alternatively, Constellation seeks rehearing on this

issue. Constellation also requests that the Commission clarify the filing of an Interim Network

Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) application by an applicant with a pending NITS

application does not restart the NITS process, sending the applicant to the “back of the line.”

                     STATEMENT OF ISSUES/SPECIFICATIONS OF ERROR

           In accordance with section 713 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,6

Constellation respectfully submits the following statement of issues and specifications of error:

               1. The June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because it fails to
                  meaningfully address Constellation’s comments that a replacement rate for the new
                  transmission services must include study deadlines. The June 2026 Co-Location
                  Order is also arbitrary and capricious because its failure to establish study deadlines
                  for the new transmission services is inconsistent with the contemporaneously issued
                  ANOPR Show Cause Order requiring study deadlines for the provision of
                  transmission service for large loads, and the Commission fails to acknowledge this
                  inconsistency. Each of these shortcomings renders the June 2026 Co-Location
                  Order arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); Motor Vehicle Mfrs.
                  Ass’n of U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (“State
                  Farm”); New England Power Generators Ass’n v. FERC, 881 F.3d 202, 210-11
                  (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“NEPGA”).

               2. The June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because it fails to
                  explain why Necessary Studies provisions that determine required upgrades—and
                  therefore significantly affect the rates, terms, and conditions of service—may be




6
    18 C.F.R. § 385.713(c)(1)-(2).

                                                     3
                     relegated to unenforceable PJM Manuals rather than included in the Tariff. See 5
                    U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.

               3. The June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because its finding
                  that suspending new transmission service for an Eligible Customer up to 120 days
                  after the first misoperation of control technologies and/or protection systems is just
                  and reasonable is not adequately supported by the facts, is logically inconsistent
                  with the Commission’s finding that PJM’s one-strike proposal for failing to follow
                  a curtailment or load shed directive is “unnecessarily strict,” and fails to engage
                  with Constellation’s arguments that a 120-day suspension is not consistent with
                  existing practice. Each of these shortcomings render the June 2026 Co-Location
                  Order arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); State Farm, 463 U.S. at
                  43; Burlington Truck Lines v. United States, 371 U.S. 156, 168 (1962)
                  (“Burlington”); NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 210-11.

               4. The June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because it confers
                  unfettered discretion upon the Transmission Owners with respect to necessary
                  control technologies and protection systems without consideration of comments
                  advising otherwise. Failure to consider comments raised renders the June 2026 Co-
                  Location Order arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); State Farm, 463
                  U.S. at 43; NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 210-11.

               5. If the Commission does not clarify the definition of Co-Located Generating
                  Facility, the June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because it
                  fails to provide a logical basis for denying Constellation’s request that only the
                  portion of the Generating Facility serving the Co-Located Load be considered the
                  Co-Located Generating Facility. Failure to consider comments raised renders the
                  June 2026 Co-Location Order arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A);
                  State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43; NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 210-11.

                                       REQUEST FOR REHEARING

     I.    The Commission Should Require Study Deadlines Binding Both PJM and the
           Transmission Owners.

           The June 2026 Co-Location Order fails to engage with repeated requests for the

Commission to direct PJM and the Transmission Owners to establish and comply with study

deadlines for the new transmission services, which are imperative for the speedy interconnection

of large loads.7 The Commission “decline[d] to direct PJM to provide more detail in its Tariff on



7
    See, e.g., Constellation Apr. 24 Response Brief at 2 (“Two simple solutions can prevent discrimination and delay:
    first, deadlines for deliverables from the Transmission Owners, such as studies, and second, requiring standards,


                                                          4
 the process for studying requests for Interim NITS”—but did not provide any discussion of study

deadlines.8 For Firm Contract Demand Service and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, the

Commission directed that PJM adopt more precise terms and conditions similar to “the cluster

study process” and study procedures in the Non-Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service,9

respectively, but also did not require study deadlines. The lack of study deadlines and any mention

of them is a failure to engage in reasoned decision making and bad policy.

            First, failure to engage with comments raised is a violation of the Administrative Procedure

Act (“APA”).10 Summarizing comments is not sufficient.11 The Commission must take the next

step of providing a substantive response to the comments raised.

            Second, the absence of binding and enforceable deadlines for the new transmission services

is inconsistent with the June 2026 Co-Location Order itself, where the Commission acknowledged

establish one. The lack of study deadlines is also inconsistent with the Commission’s preliminary

finding in the contemporaneously issued ANOPR Show Cause Order that PJM’s Tariff is unjust

and unreasonable because it lacks “a study deadline of no more than 60-90 calendar days” for

transmission service requests by Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads.13 The June 2026 Co-

animating the ANOPR Show Cause Order study deadlines are the same as those that parties have

raised in the PJM Co-Location proceeding. Failure to square precedent is a failure to engage in

reasoned decision-making.14

            Third, failure to require study deadlines binding on both PJM and the Transmission Owners

is bad policy. The delays that have plagued the Necessary Study process demonstrate this. The

absence of binding and enforceable deadlines has allowed Transmission Owners to refuse to

participate in the Necessary Study process and delay the interconnection of large loads for years.15

 Deadlines binding only PJM, but not the Transmission Owners, have failed to produce the timely

completion of studies. Indeed, PJM’s Form of Necessary Studies Agreement provides that PJM’s

“good faith estimate for the time of completion of Necessary Studies is within 270 days,” or just

less than 9 months, from the date that PJM “approves the dynamic model and data submitted by

Project Developer.”16 Yet (and aside from the inconsistency with the 60 to 90 day timing in the

ANOPR Show Cause Order), Constellation has been waiting years for Necessary Studies for

multiple projects, where the Transmission Owner simply refused to cooperate with PJM. New

transmission service requests will be subject to the same delays unless the Commission requires

PJM to establish and enforce deadlines that bind both PJM and the Transmission Owners.

             Using its authority to establish a just and reasonable replacement rate,17 the Commission

should modify its June 2026 Co-Location Order to require PJM to establish such study deadlines.

Requiring PJM to establish a deadline would not constrain PJM’s discretion in determining how

best to maintain the reliability of the transmission system. PJM would remain free to propose

appropriate deadlines, provided those deadlines are reasonable.

            The Commission also should require PJM to establish Necessary Study deadlines binding

both PJM and the Transmission Owners. While the December 2025 Co-Location Order did not

direct revisions to the Necessary Study process,18 the Commission has the authority to modify its

orders before the record is filed in the court of appeals.19 Here, the record demonstrates that PJM’s

Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because the Necessary Studies provisions do not support their

timely completion.20

 II.        The Commission Should Direct PJM to Clarify its Necessary Study Process in its Tariff
            Instead of its Manual.

            In response to our argument that PJM’s proposed tariff revisions identifying the scope of

the Necessary Study Process requires “additional clarity,”21 the Commission “direct[ed] PJM to

specify in its compliance filing what types of additional detail about the studies will be available

in the PJM manuals.”22 Additional details should be included in the Tariff, not the Manuals.

             Necessary Studies, along with the methodology and process for performing them and the

results that methodology and process will produce, “significantly affect rates, terms, and

conditions”23 of generator interconnection. While including high-level descriptors of the “studies”

to be performed in the Necessary Study Process is an improvement to PJM’s current Tariff,24 PJM

must also include in the Tariff a description of the methodology and process for performing the

studies, including deadlines for completing the studies and any consultation requirements. A

framework for how Necessary Studies will be performed and completed is not a “mere

implementation detail[]”25 that may remain unenforceable and subject to unilateral change without

notice or Commission oversight.26 How studies are performed determines whether a planned

modification will have a “permanent material impact on the Transmission System” and the

upgrades to the Transmission System that are deemed “necessary.”27 And like the Tariff

requirements for studies performed for other interconnection and transmission requests,28 a

 description of the Necessary Studies methodology and process, including study and consultation

            The Necessary Study Process is a leading cause of the delay of co-located load

interconnections. The Commission should ensure rules on the Necessary Study Process are clearly

stated in the Tariff, so that everyone – transmission owners and market participants alike – know

the applicable rules, which can then be enforced by the Commission.

III.        A Two-Strike Disqualification Is a Sufficient Deterrent and Alone Should Be the Just
            and Reasonable Replacement Rate.

            The Commission failed to adequately support its finding that suspending new transmission

service for an Eligible Customer up to 120 days after the first misoperation of control technologies

and/or protection systems is just and reasonable.30 While an investigation of the misoperation is

appropriate, imposing a four-month suspension while the investigation is ongoing is not. The

Commission should reject the 120-day suspension and approve only the two-strike disqualification

penalty for the misoperation of control technologies and/or protection systems as the just and

reasonable operational penalty.

            First, suspending service for an Eligible Customer for 120 days will have no added

deterrence value or reliability benefit on top of imposing a two-strike disqualification penalty.31 A

two-strike disqualification penalty will sufficiently incentivize Co-Located Loads to make sure

they are “willing and able to limit their energy withdrawals.”32 Faced with the commercial risk

 (and potential commercial penalties) of disqualification and the years-long NITS process,33 Co-

Located Loads will seek to ensure they do not cause or allow the misoperation of necessary control

technologies and/or protections schemes. Imposing a 120-day suspension regardless of the Eligible

Facility’s or load’s fault, will not make loads or Eligible Customers any more diligent. In fact,

given the increased risk and uncertainty, loads that are otherwise willing and able to limit their

withdrawals could be deterred from applying for the new transmission services and, instead, elect

NITS, leading to “unnecessary transmission system buildout.”34

            Nor do the North American Electric Reliability Corporation’s (“NERC”) reliability

standards require suspension of service when a protection scheme misoperates today. NERC

reliability standards require that the misoperation be investigated and a corrective action plan

developed.35 If the Commission believes more should be required to ensure reliability, it can direct

NERC to evaluate and establish reliability standards through the ordinary statutory process.

            Second, the Commission’s approval of the 120-day suspension is logically inconsistent

with its finding that PJM’s one-strike proposal for failing to follow a curtailment or load shed

 directive is “unnecessarily strict.”36 A four-month loss of transmission service—that has the

potential to be economically ruinous—effectively amounts to a one-strike proposal.37 If

disqualification after the first failure to follow a load shed or curtailment directive is “unnecessarily

strict,” so too should a four-month disqualification for the misoperation of control technologies

and/or protection systems that may be unrelated to actions taken by the load or Eligible Customer.

            Third, the Commission’s finding failed to consider arguments Constellation raised in its

May 11 Answer.38 Our May 11 Answer explained that PJM’s claim its 120-day suspension was

“consistent” with NERC requirements was incorrect, stating, “[t]he NERC Reliability Standards

that PJM cites—PRC-004-6 (Protection System Misoperation Identification and Correction) and

PRC-012-2 (Remedial Action Schemes)—set forth a process for investigating whether protection

systems misoperated and for developing a Corrective Action Plan if appropriate” but neither

reliability standard “call[ed] for suspension or disqualification of service while an investigation is

ongoing.”39 While the Commission summarizes our comments,40 the Commission does not

provide a substantive response.41 Failure to respond to comments raised is an APA violation.42

             If the Commission denies our request for rehearing, the Commission should clarify that an

Eligible Customer could still take transmission service on behalf of other loads during the

suspension period. This change is necessary to make the suspension and disqualification provisions

consistent. The June 2026 Co-Location Order found it not just and reasonable to “disqualify the

Eligible Customer as a whole from taking the relevant transmission service” after the two strikes

and directed PJM to revise its Tariff to allow the Eligible Customer to “still take transmission

service, including Interim NITS, FCD transmission service, and NFCD transmission service, on

behalf of other loads through other transmission service agreements.”43 The same should apply to

the suspension period if the penalty is not removed.

IV.         Transmission Owners Should Not Have Unfettered Discretion over Necessary Control

suspension “following PJM’s approval, as well as the relevant transmission owner’s approval of

the necessary control technologies and/or protection systems for consistency with the transmission

owner’s technical standards.”45 Second, the Commission states, “the transmission owners shall

                                              CLARIFICATION

     I.    The Commission Should Direct PJM to Revise the Definition of Co-Located Generating
           Facility to Conform to the December 2025 Co-Location Order.

           We seek clarification on the Commission’s denial51 of Constellation’s request to revise

PJM’s definition of Co-Located Generating Facility to “mean the portion of an existing or planned

Generating Facility that the Interconnection Customer designates to serve and is physically

connected to a Co-Located Load.”52 Constellation proposed this revision to conform the definition

of Co-Located Generating Facility with the December 2025 Co-Location Order that specifically

contemplated a “portion of the generating facility [will] be designated to serve any Co-Located

Load that is not receiving NITS.”53 No party opposed. Based on these facts, it is unclear why the

Commission disagreed. The Commission should direct PJM to revise its definition on compliance.

           A more precise definition in the PJM Tariff is critical to reduce uncertainty and potential

litigation, expedite the interconnection of large loads, and ensure the intent of the December 2025

Co-Location Order is achieved. Without adding a modifier to “Generating Facility,” some could

interpret Co-Located Generating Facility as including the entire capacity at a generation site even

if only a portion of the capacity is contracted to serve the Co-Located Load. For example, where a

500-MW unit serves a 100-MW Co-Located Load, some could consider the entire 500 MW facility
